items.stem:
Study the diagram given below and answer the questions that follow:
(i) Name the defect of vision represented in the diagram. Give reason for your answer.
(ii) List two causes of this defect.
(iii) With the help of a diagram show how this defect of vision is corrected.
items.answer:
(i) The defect is hypermetropia (far-sightedness), because the far point is still situated at infinity but the near point has shifted away from D = 25 cm.
(ii) Causes of hypermetropia: (a) the focal length of the eye lens is too long; (b) the eye ball has become too small.
(iii) A convex lens of suitable focal length is required to correct this defect. The converging lens forms the image of a nearby object at the shifted near point, so that the eye lens can then focus it on the retina.

items.stem:
(a) Ravi kept a book at a distance of 10 cm from the eyes of his friend Hari. Hari is not able to read anything written on the book. Explain why.
(b) A lens of focal length 5.0 cm is being used by a student in the laboratory as a magnifying glass. His least distance of distinct vision is 25 cm. What magnification is the student getting?
items.answer:
(a) Because the least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye is 25 cm. A book held only 10 cm away lies closer than the near point, so the eye lens cannot form a distinct image of it on the retina and Hari cannot read the writing.
(b) Given f = 5 cm, v = −25 cm (image formed at the near point), u = ?
1/v − 1/u = 1/f
1/u = 1/v − 1/f = (−1/25) − (1/5) = (−1 − 5)/25 = −6/25
u = −25/6 cm
m = v/u = (−25)/(−25/6) = (−25 × 6)/(−25) = 6
The student is getting a magnification of 6.
items.ocr: The LaTeX block for part (b) was badly mangled by MinerU — the rows '1/f', '1/u', '1/u', '1/u' are printed empty of their right-hand sides. The chain was reconstructed from the surviving printed values u = −25/6 cm and m = v/u = (−25 × 6)/(−25), which give m = 6.

items.stem: Why is Tyndall effect shown by colloidal particles? State four instances of observing the Tyndall effect.
items.answer:
Tyndall effect is shown by colloidal particles because they scatter light. Scattering of light is the change in the direction of light on striking an obstacle (atom, molecule, dust particle, smoke, water droplet, etc.). When a beam of light strikes such fine particles, the path of the light becomes visible. This phenomenon of scattering of light by colloidal particles is the Tyndall effect.
Four instances where the Tyndall effect can be observed:
1. When a fine beam of sunlight enters a smoke-filled room, the smoke particles become visible due to scattering of light by these particles.
2. When sunlight passes through the canopy of a dense forest, the tiny water droplets in the mist scatter the light.
3. Milk is a colloid that contains globules of fat and protein. When a beam of light is directed at a glass of milk the light is scattered — a good example of the Tyndall effect.
4. Blue colour of the clear sky: the scattering of the blue component of white light by the air molecules present in the atmosphere causes the blue colour of the sky.
items.ocr: Printed 'tiny water droplets in the water scatter light' read as 'in the mist'. The p19 figure (c3feb666...) illustrates the worked solution, not the question, so it is not attached.

items.stem: Explain, how the power of accommodation of human eye is achieved.
items.answer: The eye lens of the human eye is made up of a crystalline lens of variable focal length. The focal length of the human eye lens can be changed by the action of the ciliary muscles, so that images of objects placed at different positions are formed on the retina: the ciliary muscles relax for a distant object (the lens becomes thinner and its focal length increases) and contract for a nearby object (the lens becomes thicker and its focal length decreases). This ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length is called the power of accommodation.

items.stem: While sitting in the last row, a student has difficulty in reading the blackboard clearly. State the defect of vision the student is suffering from. Mention two causes of this defect. Suggest a suitable lens for the correction of this defect.
items.answer:
(i) The student is suffering from myopia or short-sightedness.
(ii) Causes of myopia: (a) the distance of the retina from the eye lens increases (elongation of the eye ball); (b) the focal length of the eye lens becomes small.
(iii) Correction of myopia: this defect can be corrected by using a concave lens of appropriate focal length.
items.ocr: The stem was split across the 6000-character dump boundary ('...correction of this def' + 'ect.') and rejoined. Printed 'a concave lens of approximate focal length' read as 'appropriate focal length'.

items.stem: A person suffering from short-sightedness can see clearly only up to a distance of 2 metres. Find the nature and power of the lens required to correct his vision.
items.answer:
A concave lens can be used to correct the vision of a myopic person.
Given v = −2 m (the person's far point), u = ∞
As we know that
1/v − 1/u = 1/f
1/(−2) − 1/∞ = 1/f
f = −2 m
P = 1/f = −1/2 = −0.5 D
So the required lens is a concave (diverging) lens of power −0.5 D.
items.ocr: Printed 'can see clearly only upon a distance of 2 metres' read as 'only up to a distance of 2 metres'.

items.stem: A person cannot see clearly objects beyond a distance of 1.2 m. Name the defect of vision he is suffering from. What would be the power of correcting lens used to restore proper vision?
items.answer:
The defect of vision is myopia (short-sightedness).
Given v = −1.2 m; u = ∞
Using the lens formula,
1/v − 1/u = 1/f
1/(−1.2) − 1/∞ = 1/f
f = −1.2 m
P = 1/f = 1/(−1.2) = −0.83 D
So a concave lens of power −0.83 D is required.

items.stem: A boy uses spectacles of focal length −60 cm. Name the defect of vision he is suffering from. Which lens is used for the correction of this defect? Compute the power of this lens.
items.answer:
The defect is myopia (short-sightedness), and a concave lens is used for its correction.
As we know, the power of a lens is given by P = 1/f
Here f = −60 cm = −60/100 m = −0.6 m
P = 1/(−0.6) D = −1.67 D
So the spectacle lens is a concave lens of power −1.67 D.
items.ocr: The printed solution drops the minus sign while converting ('f = 60 cm or 60/100 m = 0.6 m') and then stops at 'P = (1/−0.6) D' without evaluating it. The stem's f = −60 cm is authoritative, so f = −0.6 m and P = −1.67 D.

items.stem:
(a) What is hypermetropia? State two causes of hypermetropia. Draw a labelled ray diagram to show how this defect may be corrected using spectacles of appropriate focal length.
(b) The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 1.0 m. Find the power of the lens required to correct this defect. The least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye is 25 cm.
items.answer:
(a) Hypermetropia, or far-sightedness, is a defect of vision in which the affected person can see distant objects clearly but cannot see nearby objects distinctly.
Causes of hypermetropia: (i) increase in the focal length of the eye lens for near view; (ii) the eye ball becomes smaller.
Correction: a convex lens of suitable focal length placed in front of the eye converges the rays coming from an object at 25 cm so that they appear to come from the eye's own shifted near point, and the eye lens then forms the image on the retina.
(b) u = −25 cm, v = −100 cm
1/f = 1/v − 1/u = (−1/100) − (−1/25) = (−1 + 4)/100 = 3/100 cm⁻¹
f = 100/3 cm = 1/3 m
P = 1/f = +3 D
So a convex lens of power +3 D is required.

The LaTeX for (b) is garbled ('u = −25 cos', '(−25 cos) − (−100 cos)' in both numerator and denominator, '3/1 cm'); recomputed from u = −25 cm and v = −100 cm, which reproduces the printed final answer P = +3 D. The p21 figure (852d31c9...) is the solution's 'Correction for hypermetropic eye' diagram — the question asks the student to draw it — so it is not attached.

items.stem:
(a) What is myopia? State two causes of myopia. With the help of a labelled ray diagram show the correction of myopia using appropriate lens.
(b) The near point of a myopic eye is 1 m. Find the power of the lens required to correct this defect. Assume that near point of the normal eye is 25 cm.
items.answer:
(a) Myopia is a defect of vision in which the eye can see only nearby objects clearly; the image of a distant object is formed in front of the retina, so distant objects appear blurred.
Causes of myopia: (i) elongation of the eye ball; (ii) the focal length of the eye lens becomes too short.
Correction: a concave lens of suitable power diverges the rays coming from a distant object before they reach the eye lens, so that the eye lens forms the image on the retina.
(b) v = −1 m = −100 cm (the defective near point), u = −25 cm (near point of the normal eye)
1/v − 1/u = 1/f
(−1/100) − (−1/25) = 1/f
1/f = 3/100
f = 100/3 = 33.3 cm
P = 1/f = +3 D, i.e. a convex lens of power +3 D.
items.ocr: Printed number 152 (above the FIVE MARKS heading number 146) places this in the FIVE MARKS section even though MinerU prints it inside the three-marks run on p21; recorded as a 5-mark 'long' item. The stem calls it 'the near point of a myopic eye' but the printed worked solution treats the 1 m figure as a shifted NEAR point and returns a +3 D CONVEX lens, i.e. a hypermetropia-style correction — an internal contradiction in the source. Per the rule that the worked solution wins, the +3 D convex result is recorded as printed. The printed final line was OCR'd as '= 4 3 D convex | e' and read as '= +3 D convex lens'; 'f = 2' in the given list is the OCR of u = −25 cm. The p21 figure (879b3660...) belongs to the solution, so it is not attached.

items.stem:
(a) A student suffering from myopia is not able to see distinctly the objects placed beyond 5 m. List two possible reasons due to which this defect of vision have arisen. With the help of ray diagrams, explain (i) why the student is unable to see distinctly the objects placed beyond 5 m from his eyes, (ii) the type of the corrective lens used to restore proper vision and how this defect is corrected by the use of this lens.
(b) If in this case, the numerical value of the focal length of the corrective lens is 5 m, find the power of the lens as per the new cartesian sign convention.
items.answer:
(a) Two possible reasons for this defect: elongation of the eye ball (the retina moves away from the eye lens), and excessive curvature of the eye lens so that its focal length becomes too short.
(i) The student is unable to see distinctly the objects placed beyond 5 m from his eyes because he is suffering from myopia, wherein a person can see nearby objects clearly but cannot see distant objects distinctly — rays from a distant object are brought to a focus in front of the retina.
(ii) A concave lens can be used as the corrective lens to restore proper vision. A concave lens of suitable power will diverge the incoming rays and thus bring the image back on to the retina, and the defect is corrected.
(b) For a myopic eye the corrective lens is concave, so by the new cartesian sign convention f = −5 m.
P = 1/f = 1/(−5) = −0.2 D

items.stem: The near point of a person suffering from hypermetropia is 75 cm. Calculate the focal length and power of the lens required to enable him to read the newspaper which is kept at 25 cm from the eye.
items.answer:
Given u = −25 cm, v = −75 cm
As we know that
1/v − 1/u = 1/f
(−1/75) + (1/25) = 1/f
(−1 + 3)/75 = 1/f
2/75 = 1/f
f = 75/2 = 37.5 cm = 0.375 m
P = 1/f = 1000/375 = +2.67 D
So a convex lens of focal length 37.5 cm and power +2.67 D is required.

items.stem:
(i) Least distance of distinct vision of a long-sighted person is 40 cm. He wishes to reduce it to 25 cm by using spectacles. Find the power and nature of the lens used by him.
(ii) Draw a ray diagram to show the correction of the defect by using an appropriate lens.
items.answer:
(i) Given u = −25 cm, v = −40 cm
As we know that
1/f = 1/v − 1/u = (1/−40) − (1/−25) = (−5 + 8)/200 = 3/200
f = 200/3 cm
Power, P = 1/f = (100 × 3)/200 = 3/2 = +1.5 D
(ii) The lens is a convex (converging) lens of power +1.5 D. In the ray diagram the convex lens converges the rays from an object held at 25 cm so that they appear to come from 40 cm — the person's own near point — and the eye then focuses them on the retina.

items.stem: Due to gradual weakening of ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens a certain defect of vision arises. Write the name of this defect. Name the type of lens required by such persons to improve the vision. Explain the structure and function of such a lens.
items.answer:
The defect caused due to gradual weakening of the ciliary muscles and diminishing flexibility of the eye lens is presbyopia.
The type of lens required by such a person to improve the vision is a bifocal lens.
A bifocal lens consists of both a convex lens and a concave lens. Its lower part is a convex lens, which is used for reading and corrects hypermetropia, while its upper part is a concave lens, which is used for distant vision and corrects myopia.

items.stem:
(a) Draw a labelled ray diagram to show the path of a ray of light incident obliquely on one face of a glass slab.
(b) Calculate the refractive index of the material of a glass slab. Given that the speed of light through the glass slab is 2 × 10⁸ m/s and in air is 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
(c) Calculate the focal length of a lens, if its power is −2.5 D.
items.answer:
(a) In the ray diagram the ray bends towards the normal on entering the denser slab, travels in a straight line inside it, and bends away from the normal on emerging; the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced.
(b) Speed of light in the glass slab, v = 2 × 10⁸ m/s
Speed of light in air, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
Refractive index of glass, n = c/v = (3 × 10⁸)/(2 × 10⁸) = 1.5
Hence the refractive index of the material of the glass slab is 1.5.
(c) Power, P = −2.5 D; focal length, f = ?
P = 1/f
f = 1/P = 1/(−2.5) = −0.4 m, or (100 cm)/(−2.5) = −40 cm
The focal length of a lens of power −2.5 D is −0.4 m or −40 cm.

items.stem:
(a) A person suffering from myopia (near-sightedness) was advised to wear corrective lens of power −2.5 D. A spherical lens of same focal length was taken in the laboratory. At what distance should a student place an object from this lens so that it forms an image at a distance of 10 cm from the lens?
(b) Draw a ray diagram to show the position and nature of the image formed in the above case.
items.answer:
(a) P = −2.5 D, f = ?
P = 1/f ⇒ f = 1/P = 1/(−2.5 D) = −0.4 m = −40 cm
Given f = −40 cm, v = −10 cm, u = ?
1/f = 1/v − 1/u
1/u = 1/v − 1/f = (1/−10) − (1/−40) = (1/−10) + (1/40) = (−4 + 1)/40 = −3/40
u = −40/3 = −13.33 cm
The object should be placed 13.33 cm from the lens so that it forms an image at a distance of 10 cm from the lens.
(b) In the ray diagram the concave lens forms a virtual, erect and diminished image on the same side of the lens as the object, between the object and the lens.

items.stem: State the cause of dispersion of white light by a glass prism. How did Newton, using two identical glass prisms, show that white light is made of seven colours? Draw a ray diagram to show the path of a narrow beam of white light through a combination of two identical prisms arranged together in inverted position with respect to each other when it is allowed to fall obliquely on one of the faces of the first prism of the combination.
items.answer:
Light is formed of different colours which travel at their own speed inside a prism. The colours therefore bend through different angles with respect to the incident ray as they pass through the prism — the red light bends the least while the violet bends the most — and this unequal bending causes dispersion.
Newton showed that the reverse of dispersion of light is also possible. He kept two prisms close to each other, one in the erect position and the other in an inverted position. The light gets dispersed when it passes through the first prism; the second prism receives all the seven coloured rays from the first prism and combines them into the original white light. This proves that white light is made of seven colours.
items.ocr: Printed 'a narrow beam of while light' read as 'white light'. The p24 figure (3a722093...) is the solution's own two-prism diagram — the question asks the student to draw it — so it is not attached.

items.stem: What is dispersion of white light? State its cause. Draw a ray diagram to show the dispersion of white light by a glass prism.
items.answer:
Dispersion of white light: when a beam of white light is passed through a triangular glass prism, the white light splits up to form a band of seven colours on a white screen. This splitting of white light into seven colours on passing through a transparent medium like a glass prism is called dispersion of light.
Cause: the dispersion of white light occurs because the angle of refraction (or angle of deviation) of light of different colours is different when it passes through the glass prism. So when white light consisting of seven colours passes through a glass prism, each colour of it is refracted (or deviated) by a different angle, with the result that the seven colours are spread out to form a spectrum.
